ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 2 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Alexander the Great

code.originalText: Two-week review, seen the same day by pulmonology and by the clinic's addiction medicine clinician: CT of the chest, lung volumes, gas transfer and six-minute walk; chest wall pain plan; DSM-5-TR assessment and a drinking goal

text.paragraph: Two-week review, seen the same day by pulmonology and by the addiction medicine clinician. [S]

Alexander has taken acetaminophen two or three times a day, within the limit, and it takes the edge off the chest pain without stopping it; the pain is still 6 of 10 on climbs and deep breaths and wakes him when he rolls onto his left side. He has been to two banquets since intake and drank less at both, about six drinks each, and none on other days. He has had no shakes, sweats or morning drinking. He has met the behavioral health clinician once and talked about his companion for the first time. He had a CT of the chest this morning and lung volumes and a six-minute walk before this visit, and sees Dr. Abernathy-Sowande of pulmonology this afternoon. He met the clinic's addiction medicine clinician this morning. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 2026-03-23; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Well; blood pressure 128/80, pulse 76; weight 72.0 kg
Slightly reduced expansion and breath sounds at the left base; dull to percussion there; no crackles or wheeze

Healed 3 cm scar in the left fourth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line; tenderness along the fifth rib and the intercostal space below the scar; a 4 by 3 cm area of allodynia around the scar
Engaged; sad when he speaks of his companion; no thoughts of suicide

Left chest wall pain at the scar of an old penetrating arrow wound, with breathlessness on exertion and a reduced FVC (78 percent predicted) with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio, and heavy episodic drinking (AUDIT 19, PEth 236 ng/mL), found at intake; cause and extent under evaluation with a pulmonology consultation and an addiction medicine assessment

S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to the documented chest wound and the documented drinking parties; superseded at the consultation, when the chest wall pain, the pleural thickening and the alcohol use disorder were diagnosed.
Chronic post-traumatic chest wall pain: intercostal neuropathic pain at the healed left chest wound and fifth rib fracture, with tenderness and a small area of allodynia over the scar
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, anchored to the documented arrow wound; not a claim about his real chest.

Localized left pleural thickening (fibrothorax) from an old organized hemothorax after a penetrating chest wound, with a mild restrictive defect (TLC 79 percent predicted) and normal gas transfer; no retained foreign body, fistula or trapped lung on CT
S — Synthetic modern finding of the CT and lung function tests at the consultation, anchored to the documented arrow wound; the retrospective pneumothorax (CLM-0004) is not used.

Alcohol use disorder, mild (three DSM-5-TR criteria): drinking more than intended at banquets, riding after drinking, and arguments with his officers while drunk; ten or more drinks on two or three nights a week, more since his bereavement; no withdrawal; AUDIT 19; PEth 236 ng/mL

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made with the addiction medicine clinician at the consultation visit, anchored to the documented drinking parties; the criteria, amounts and scores are synthetic. The diagnosis is mild, in keeping with the disputed evidence (CLM-0008).

Bereavement five months after the death of his closest companion since boyhood, with depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 12, item 9 scored 0) that do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode; prolonged grief disorder cannot be diagnosed before twelve months
S — Synthetic modern assessment anchored to the documented bereavement; DSM-5-TR codes uncomplicated bereavement as Z63.4 whatever the relationship. Not a claim about his real mental health.

list.item:
Chronic post-traumatic chest wall pain (G89.21). Dr. Abernathy-Sowande agrees that the pain is intercostal neuropathic pain at the healed wound and rib fracture, not pleural or cardiac pain. Opioids, tramadol, gabapentinoids and benzodiazepines are avoided while he drinks heavily. [S]
Lidocaine 5% patch over the scar for up to 12 hours a day from today.
Continue acetaminophen within 2,000 mg a day.
Telephone check on the patch in four weeks.
An intercostal nerve block if pain stays above 4 of 10 after six weeks.

Localized left fibrothorax after an old hemothorax (J94.1). Localized pleural thickening with a mild restrictive defect from outside the lung (TLC 79 percent, normal DLCO with a high KCO) and a normal six-minute walk; no retained fragment, fistula or trapped lung. Decortication is not indicated. [S]
Physical therapy for thoracic mobility and scar desensitization, deep-breathing exercises, and graded training back to long marches.
Repeat spirometry in about two months.

Alcohol use disorder, mild (F10.10). With the addiction medicine clinician this morning: three DSM-5-TR criteria (more than intended, riding after drinking, and arguments while drunk), a mild disorder. No withdrawal risk with his pattern. He chose a moderation goal: no more than four drinks on any day and fourteen in a week, two alcohol-free days, and no riding or driving after drinking. Naltrexone was offered; he declined for now. [S]
Sessions with the addiction medicine clinician every two weeks.
PEth and liver tests at six weeks.
Naltrexone offered again if he cannot keep the goal.

Bereavement with depressive symptoms (Z63.4). Grief five months after his companion's death, with sadness and poor sleep. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide or self-harm; service pistol in the armory off duty; 988 card carried. [S]
Behavioral health sessions every two weeks.
PHQ-9 at six weeks.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: ERS/ATS technical standard on interpretive strategies for routine lung function tests (2022); British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease (2023); CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (2022); The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Substance Use Disorders (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression monograph (2026); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024)

Follow-up: Six-week review with PEth, liver tests, PHQ-9 and a pain score. Telephone check on the patch in four weeks. Physical therapy weekly; addiction medicine and behavioral health every two weeks. The clinic or 988 at any hour. Next scheduled visit 2026-04-20: six-week review: chest wall pain and the exercise program, drinking and PEth, liver tests, grief and mood, safety, and the healed forearm wound. [S]
